I know that perpetual motion cannot exist. I'm just looking for the flaw in this system:

0) Construct a very tall silo of water (ex: 6 feet in diameter, 1000 feet tall).

1) place a very heavy, but buoyant object in the bottom of the silo (lifting the object to the top of the silo)

2) push the object off the side of the silo, and allow it to turn a turbine or something.

3) put the object back in the bottom of the silo; repeat.

It seems like there is an incredible amount of "free" energy to be harnessed from allowing the buoyant object to float to the top of the silo, increasing it's potential energy. Where is this energy expended that would invalidate the premise of this machine?
Why wouldn't this perpetual motion machine work?
Step 3 - pushing the float back to the bottom of the silo would require outside energy.

I understand that loading the float into the silo would require some energy, as would pushing it off the side of the silo, but can't that be overcome by just making the silo taller, therefore generating more energy when dropping it? It will take the same amount of energy to load the float into a 30ft silo as it would a 3000ft silo. Or am I missing something?

Actually, it would take more energy to push the float down into a longer silo.

The thing is, when you first push the float to the bottom of the water, you are using outside energy to do so, and storing kinetic energy in the float. However, all that kinetic energy is used up once the float rises back to the top of the water. You then need more outside energy to push the float over the side, where you will use gravitational energy on its way down, and that is all gone once it hits the ground. And now you're right back at the beginning - you need to somehow get the float back under water at the bottom of the silo, but you've exhausted all your potential energy at this point... so, you are back to needing outside energy yet again.

It's basically like rolling a ball down a hill - once you reach the bottom, you have to spend energy to get it back to the top. In your case, its the opposite, once the float gets to the top of the water, you have to spend energy to get it back down to the bottom.

when you first push the float to the bottom of the water

I am not suggesting that we start at the top and push it down, I'm suggesting we load it into the bottom of the silo. Forcing it in against the immense pressure in the silo would waste energy, but perhaps the silo can be built on top of a lake, and (temporarily) capped at the top (like holding your thumb over a straw and pulling it almost all the way out of your drink will allow the water to stay in your straw. All you have to do is force the float down far enough to get into the open bottom of the silo (a few feet down), and then buoyancy will raise it 1000 times higher than that.
How do you load it into the bottom of the silo without the water draining out?
Capping the top of the silo was my original idea, but I've been told this won't work at that height. So, I guess that method won't work.
A vacuum can only hold water up to about 10m. Siphons don't work past this height because a cavity forms in the water. The height depends on the vapour pressure of the liquid.

Though that specific description wouldn't work in earth-like conditions (requires large atmospheric pressure), here's why the principle is invalid:

The object has a volume, displacing some water (this is why buoyancy happens). So here's what happens:

1.The object falls, it releases energy

2.Raising the silo requires much more energy

3.Lowering the silo again releases energy, but less than raising it, because the object now in the bottom of the silo is taking up room so not all the water is coming back down.

The object floating to the surface transfers energy to it which is released in the fall step, and that energy would bring the total energy balance to 0 if everything was 100% efficient.

Because loading the buoyant object would take more energy than loading a neutral object. This is because the pressure at the base of the silo. An example of a neutral object would be water, which reduces the system to a pump and fountain.
